_readme: Massrofy bundled parser rule pack — docs/architecture.md ADR-007 / §5.2 Contract A.
THIS FILE IS DATA, NOT CODE. Adding a bank or a message type means editing this
file; it must never mean editing lib/features/parsing/. That is the whole point of
ADR-007 (NFR-M1), and it is the acceptance bar on Linear KHA-19.
NFR-M3 — every pattern here was authored from the STRUCTURAL descriptions in
docs/PRD.md §3.4. No genuine bank SMS was copied into this file, and none may be.
Bank names are real (they are public companies), but every template, amount,
merchant, account suffix, reference number and date in the matching fixture corpus
is invented. See test/fixtures/synthetic_sms_corpus.dart.
Rules are matched in DESCENDING priority, first match wins (§5.2). The ignore rules
sit at 900 so an OTP that happens to contain a transaction keyword is recognised as
an OTP first (AC-A2.1) — get that ordering wrong and the app invents a purchase out
of a security code. The bare 'debited from account' rules sit at 100 so every more
specific debit template (fee, installment, bill, repayment) is tried before the
catch-all.
Note on `network` values: they are extracted verbatim from the message, so the
Arabic-language bank yields Arabic tokens. Canonicalising those onto the
visa|mada|mastercard vocabulary in architecture §4.2 is P3 entity-resolution work,
not a parser concern — the parser's job is to report what the message said.
=== KHA-128: senderPatterns are HUMAN-CONFIRMED, not inferred =============
The original `senderPatterns` for the two banks below were written from assumption
(`^(BAJ|Aljazira|AlJazira|BankAlJazira)$`, `^(D360|D360Bank|D-360)$`) and matched
NOTHING on a real device: the sender ids actually shown are `Jazira Bank` and
`D360 Bank`, with a space. Every message from both banks was therefore discarded at
gate 1 as a non-financial sender — silently, and by design, because NFR-P4 keeps no
trace of an unmatched sender. The user saw 0.00 SAR and an empty review queue.
So: the sender id is the one field in this file that MUST NOT be guessed. These
seven strings were read off the reporting user's phone and confirmed on KHA-128 on
2026-07-30: `Jazira Bank`, `nera`, `D360 Bank`, `AlRajhi Bank`, `STC Bank`, `SAIB`,
`SAB`. The earlier guessed alternatives are KEPT rather than replaced — an unused
alternative is dead weight, a missing one loses a financial message.
Two deliberate choices in how they are written:
- `\s*` between a brand's own words (`^D360\s*Bank$`) rather than one literal
space. `\s` also covers the non-breaking space an Arabic-locale device can
deliver, and the no-space spelling. Widening WITHIN one brand's own words is
safe: `^...$` anchoring means a false positive needs a whole sender id equal to
that brand, and the cost of a miss is a silently dropped transaction.
- `^STC\s*Bank$` deliberately does NOT match a bare `STC`, which is the telecom
operator, not the bank. Case is irrelevant everywhere: the loader compiles every
pattern with `caseSensitive: false`.
Scope of that confirmation, stated so nothing here looks more verified than it is:
only the SENDER IDS were read off a device. Each bank's `displayName` and `aliases`
come from public branding, and the Arabic display names for `nera` and `stc bank` are
transliterations of a Latin-script brand rather than confirmed official strings. That
is a much smaller risk than a wrong sender pattern and it is not the same kind of
claim: identity is `bankId` and nothing else (AC-B12.3), and a display string is only
ever an input to name lookup — a wrong one shows a wrong label, it cannot lose a
message. Correct them freely; never repoint a `bankId`, which is persisted.
=== A sender with `messageRules: []` is a COMPLETE state, not a stub =====
A bank may declare a confirmed sender and NO parsing templates. That is a complete,
shippable state — AC-A6.5 (PRD Addendum A, approved): a sender that passes gate 1
with no matching template lands in the Needs Review queue with its sanitised text,
where US-A4/S-19 completes it by hand. Concretely, an empty `messageRules` list makes
the engine's rule loop iterate zero times and fall through to its step 4 branch —
`UnparsedMessage(noRuleMatched)` — which is the same path a configured bank takes
when it changes a template. So a recognised sender is useful IMMEDIATELY with zero
rules written, and `test/features/ingestion/sender_only_bank_review_test.dart`
proves it end to end rather than at the data level only.
`saib` is in exactly that state today, deliberately: no message sample of any kind
has been observed for it. Do not invent templates for it to make this file look
finished — a guessed extraction regex silently writes a WRONG AMOUNT, which is the
one failure this product cannot survive. A missing template only costs a manual
completion, which the user can see and fix.
=== KHA-136 / KHA-145: templates written from live structural specs =======
On 2026-07-30 the human read the shapes of their real messages off their own device
and described them STRUCTURALLY on KHA-136 — field names, field order, language,
delimiter style, which sub-fields exist, which fields are sometimes absent. No real
message text, amount, name, merchant or account number was recorded anywhere,
including in that issue (NFR-M3). Every pattern below was authored from those
descriptions, and every matching fixture value in
`test/fixtures/synthetic_sms_corpus.dart` is invented.
What that round covered, and what it deliberately did NOT:
- `nera`      — one card-purchase type. No OTP/marketing sample, so no ignore rule.
- `stc-bank`  — SARIE inward transfer, internal transfer out, a P2P `Pay X`
payment, and OTPs (two ignore rules — see stc-payment-otp).
- `sab`       — the SAME purchase type in BOTH English and Arabic (this bank sends
either), an Arabic incoming-transfer deposit, and an Arabic
biometric-login notification (ignore).
- `al-rajhi`  — an OTP only. It gets an ignore rule and NO transaction rule,
because no transaction sample was obtained. That gap is expected
and is tracked, not papered over.
- `bank-aljazira` / `d360` — already templated, and STILL missing message types:
a second (wallet/channel-branded) Arabic POS variant and a
beneficiary notification for Aljazira; an incoming-transfer
notification, an Ecommerce purchase and an Arabic OTP for D360.
"Configured" never meant "complete" (KHA-145).
`requiredFields` stays at [amount, occurredAt] on every transaction rule, matching
the rules that were already here. That is deliberate and KHA-145 is the reason: the
Aljazira variant below reached the review queue as "some details were missing"
because a real message did not carry every field a rule demanded. A field that is
sometimes absent (a running balance, a card network, a wallet tag, a reference)
must be OPTIONAL in the regex and absent from `requiredFields` — it then reads as
explicitly unknown (AC-B1.3) instead of blocking the parse.

_note: KHA-145. A beneficiary-registration / pending-activation notice: it names a
payee and often a waiting period, and it moves NO money. Without this rule it
sits in Needs Review forever, where the only honest thing the user can do is
delete it one by one.
`intent: ignore` is not the same as dropping it. Per NFR-P4 / ADR-015 the
engine still writes a counter row with `sanitizedBody = NULL`, so the
parser-health panel can say "we saw 6 of these this month" while retaining
not one character of the text. Recognised-and-discarded, never silently gone.
P3b-1 (KHA-28). A refund is a CREDIT and reduces spend (US-B7, AC-B7.1).
It sits above the purchase rules because a refund message names a card and
an amount just as a purchase does; if the purchase rule were tried first on
a bank that ever wrote 'شراء' in a reversal, a refund would be added to
spend instead of subtracted from it — an error of twice the amount.
affectsSpend is TRUE: a refund does affect the spend total, negatively.
P3b-1 (KHA-29, AC-B10.2). Cash out of an ATM is NOT spend: the money is
still the user's, it has merely stopped being traceable. Counting it as
spend would double-count every cash purchase the user later enters by hand
(US-B4). affectsSpend is false, and `spend_classification.dart` reports it
on its own line rather than folding it anywhere.
P3b-1 (KHA-29, AC-B10.1). Salary is income, not spend, and it gets its own
messageType so the income view can name it — PRD §3.4 observed salary
arriving as an incoming transfer, so this rule sits ABOVE transfer_in and a
message that says neither 'راتب' nor 'حوالة واردة' still falls through to
the generic incoming-transfer rule rather than being lost.
KHA-145 — the SECOND Aljazira POS channel. Real messages of this shape were
sitting in the user's Needs Review queue reading "Some details were missing
from this message", which is the tell: they passed `baj-pos-purchase-ar`'s
gate (they do say شراء / بطاقة / لدى) and then failed its extraction, because
this channel prints a DIFFERENT date format and adds an available-balance and
a total-amount-due line the older template never had.
Priority 555 — above `baj-pos-purchase-ar` (550) — is the whole fix. Both
gates match this message; first match wins; so the specific variant must be
tried first or the generic rule swallows it and fails again. The gate keys on
the balance/amount-due lines rather than on a payment-brand name: the brand
is exactly the part a bank can rebrand next quarter, while an account summary
line is the structural difference.
`الرصيد المتاح` and `إجمالي المستحق` are BOTH optional in the regex even
though the gate needs one of them, because a variant that drops one must
still parse rather than regress into review — the KHA-145 failure mode.
The total-amount-due figure is captured and deliberately NOT extracted: it is
a statement balance, not a movement, and `ParsedFields` has no field for it.
Writing it into `remainingBalance` alongside the available balance would put
two different numbers in one slot.
`(?:ال)?` in front of the Arabic labels absorbs the definite article: this
channel prints `المبلغ:` where the older template prints `مبلغ:`, and that one
two-letter prefix is enough on its own to make an extraction regex miss.
KHA-145. D360 writes its transaction messages in English but sends the
verification code for an online purchase in ARABIC, so `d360-otp`'s English
keyword list never saw it. The message quotes the purchase it is confirming —
merchant, amount and all — which makes it the exact AC-A2.1 hazard: at any
lower priority a rule could read a security code as a second purchase and
double the user's spend for that day. 900 puts it above every transaction
rule, and the corpus pins a fixture whose body contains a full purchase.

messageRules._note: P3b-1 (KHA-28) — see the note on baj-refund-ar.
P3b-1 (KHA-29, AC-B10.2) — see the note on baj-atm-withdrawal-ar.
P3b-1 (KHA-29, AC-B10.1) — see the note on baj-salary-ar.

_note: KHA-145 — D360's Ecommerce purchase, a THIRD purchase shape alongside the
`purchase of …` (POS) and `online purchase of …` (FX) templates already here.
It is a label:value layout with an explicit `Ecommerce` channel tag and, in
the sample described, no conversion or fee block at all — so it is a distinct
template, not a widening of `d360-online-purchase-en`, whose regex requires
the parenthesised converted amount, the FX fee and the rate.
`messageType` is `online_purchase` and not a new `ecommerce_purchase` string:
the type vocabulary is closed (`lib/features/ledger/transaction_types.dart`),
and a type this build does not know is excluded from spend totals until
something classifies it. An unrecognised type would make a real purchase
invisible in the one number the product exists to show.
Card network and card type are optional in the regex: a card can be printed
with neither, and requiring them would push a genuine purchase into review.
KHA-145 — D360's incoming-transfer NOTIFICATION, a second inbound shape
alongside `d360-transfer-in-en`. It leads with the sending bank, names the
sender and the sender's masked IBAN, and carries no `Ref` field, so the
existing rule's regex cannot read it.
sign `credit`, affectsSpend `false`. Money arriving is not spending, and if
the counterparty turns out to be the user themselves the P3 internal-transfer
pairing (US-B10/B11) nets it against the matching outbound leg. Getting this
flag wrong is not cosmetic: `true` here would ADD every incoming transfer to
the spend total, which for a salary-sized credit is the largest possible
error in the only number the product exists to show.
The IBAN is captured and deliberately NOT extracted. It identifies the
COUNTERPARTY, and the only instrument fields available (`instrumentRef` /
`settlementRef`) mean "the user's own card or account" — a transaction is
attributed to whatever they name (AC-B13.1/2, `instrument_identity.dart`).
Writing a stranger's IBAN there would invent an account in the user's own
bank tree and attribute their money to it. Better a field we cannot store
than a field stored in the wrong place.
KHA-136. ONE message type was observed for nera: an English card purchase in a
label:value layout, whose `Card:` value is a semicolon-joined list of sub-fields
ending in the masked number, with an OPTIONAL running balance line.
One type is therefore all this bank gets. No OTP, marketing or balance-info
sample was seen, so nera has no `ignore` rules — an ignore rule keyed on guessed
keywords would either never fire (dead weight) or fire on something it should
not (a discarded transaction). Everything unmatched still reaches Needs Review
(AC-A6.5), which is the honest place for a message nobody has described yet.
The `Card:` sub-fields are semicolon-joined and their COUNT varies — a wallet
tag may or may not be present in front of the network. So `net` is written as
"everything up to the LAST semicolon" (`[^:]+` is greedy and backtracks to
it) and the masked number is what follows. That reads a two-part or a
three-part list with one pattern instead of guessing the arity.
`Balance:` is optional — the structural spec says a running balance is not on
every message — and it lands in `remainingBalance`, which `ParsedFields`
documents as informational and never treats as spend. Two fixtures pin both
shapes, because "optional" that is only ever tested present is not optional.
KHA-136. The ONLY AlRajhi sample obtained was an OTP — a two-line English
"OTP Code / Reason" message. So this bank gets an ignore rule and NOTHING else.
That is a deliberate, useful half-step, not an oversight: the OTPs stop
accumulating in Needs Review (they become counter-only rows, NFR-P4), while a
genuine AlRajhi transaction — whose shape nobody has yet described — still lands
in the queue where the user can see and complete it. Writing a transaction
template here from imagination is the one thing that would be worse than
waiting: an extraction regex that half-fits produces a WRONG amount silently,
whereas a missing one produces a visible review item.
KHA-136. Four message types were described for STC Bank, all English, all in a
one-label-per-line layout with NO colons — the labels themselves are the
delimiters, which is why these regexes key on `amount`, `from`, `to account`
and so on as words rather than on punctuation.
The important one is the P2P pair. A `Pay X` payment arrives as TWO separate
SMS — the payment confirmation and its own OTP — for ONE logical transaction,
and the OTP half quotes the payee and the amount. If both became transactions
the user's spend would be exactly doubled for that payment. They are not merged
into one rule (the engine parses one message at a time, and pairing two SMS is
not something a rule pack can express); instead `stc-payment-otp` recognises
the OTP half at priority 910 and discards its body, so the pair yields exactly
one transaction. `stc-p2p-payment-en` also carries the OTP keywords in its
`noneOf` — belt and braces, because the cost of getting this wrong is a
double-counted amount and the cost of the extra clause is nothing.
The OTP half of a `Pay X` pair: it names the payee and the amount, so it is
the most dangerous message this bank sends. Priority 910 puts it above the
generic OTP rule purely so the parser-health panel can count the two
separately; both are `ignore`, so a mix-up would be harmless — which is
exactly why the ordering that DOES matter (ignore above transaction) is
asserted in `rule_pack_corpus_test.dart` rather than left to reading.
SARIE is Saudi Arabia's interbank transfer system, so this is money arriving
from ANOTHER bank. credit, and affectsSpend false — see the note on
`d360-transfer-in-notification-en` for why that flag is the one to get right.
The gate keys on `sarie` alone: it is unambiguous, it appears in no other
message type, and a narrow gate on a distinctive token beats a wide gate that
has to be fenced off with exclusions.
An instant transfer out to a named recipient. `affectsSpend: true` matches
every other `transfer_out` rule in this pack: money leaving toward a named
counterparty IS spend unless the counterparty turns out to be the user, and
that is a property of the PAIR, which P3's internal-transfer matcher decides
(US-B11, AC-B11.2). A single rule looking at a single message cannot know it,
and guessing `false` here would silently hide real payments from the total.
The gate requires the `amount` label as well as `transfer out`, so a message
that merely mentions a transfer without this layout falls through to Needs
Review instead of matching and then failing extraction — a review item that
says "we did not understand this" is more honest than one that says "details
were missing" about a rule that never applied.
The transaction half of the `Pay X` pair described in this bank's note above.
`transfer_out` rather than a new type: it is money leaving to a named person,
which is what `transfer_out` means, and the type vocabulary is closed.
KHA-136. No SAIB message of ANY kind was visible during the sampling round, so
this bank keeps its confirmed sender and zero templates — see the
"a sender with messageRules: [] is a COMPLETE state" section at the top of this
file. It is the control case for that claim, and
`test/features/ingestion/sender_only_bank_review_test.dart` still proves it end
to end. Revisit when the user has SAIB activity to describe.
KHA-136. SAB is the BILINGUAL case, and it is the reason this pack cannot
assume one language per bank: the SAME purchase type was observed from this one
sender in English AND in Arabic, with different punctuation conventions in each
(semicolon-joined card sub-fields in English, a parenthesised network in
Arabic). Both get their own rule. Writing only the language that happened to
arrive first would have left half of this bank's purchases in Needs Review with
nothing in the app to explain why some parse and some do not.
The two purchase rules sit at 550/549 — adjacent, and both above everything
else — because their gates are mutually exclusive by script, so the ordering
between them is documentation rather than logic.
A biometric/login confirmation. Not a transaction, and it must be recognised
as such at a HIGH priority rather than left unmatched: it is security-shaped
text from a financial sender, and the next loosely-written rule anyone adds
to this bank is exactly the kind that would try to read one as a movement.
English POS purchase. The `Card:` value is a semicolon-joined list — masked
number first, then the network, then a wallet tag — and BOTH trailing
sub-fields are optional, so a message that prints only the number still
parses. The wallet tag is captured and not extracted: `InstrumentReference`
has `network` and `cardType` (credit|debit|prepaid) and a wallet is neither.
`Balance:` is optional. The structural spec is explicit that not every SAB
purchase carries a running balance, and that is precisely the shape of the
KHA-145 defect on the other bank — a field required by a rule but absent
from a real message routes a genuine purchase to Needs Review forever.
The SAME purchase type in Arabic. Same fields, Arabic labels, and the
network in parentheses instead of semicolon-joined — so it needs its own
pattern, not a widened English one. The Arabic labels are matched by their
STEMS (`بطاقة`, `مبلغ`, `رصيد`, `تاريخ`) so the definite article `ال` a bank
may or may not print costs nothing.
The network here is extracted verbatim in Arabic, per this file's standing
note: canonicalising it onto visa|mada|mastercard is P3 entity-resolution
work, and the parser's job is to report what the message said. It is safe
for it to differ between languages because the network is an ATTRIBUTE of an
instrument, never part of its identity — identity is bank + kind + digits
(`instrument_identity.dart`), so the same card seen in both languages stays
one card.
Arabic incoming-transfer deposit. credit / affectsSpend false, for the
reasons spelled out on `d360-transfer-in-notification-en`.
The masked account it names is the USER'S receiving account, so that one IS
extracted as `instrumentRef`. The sender's IBAN is captured and NOT extracted
— it belongs to the counterparty, and there is no field for it that would not
misattribute it to the user. The IBAN, the sender bank and the reference are
all optional in the pattern: any of them missing must cost a nullable field,
never the transaction.
